paragraphs: A differentiable optimization layer lets a machine learning system use the solution of a mathematical optimization problem as part of its computation. Training then requires tracking how that solution changes when its inputs change. Existing methods commonly do this through implicit differentiation, which can require expensive second-order information involving Hessians.

This paper recasts the task as bilevel optimization: one optimization problem sits inside another. It constructs an active-set Lagrangian proxy to estimate the hypergradient, the gradient needed to train through the inner problem. The estimate uses only first-order information, with a requirement that grows logarithmically as the requested approximation becomes more accurate.

The authors also show that this gradient estimator improves the theoretical gradient complexity of constrained bilevel optimization for reaching a specified Goldstein stationarity criterion. Their implementation, FFOLayer, is a Python library designed to work with existing differentiable optimization solvers. Reported experiments show substantially faster computation with similar convergence, connecting the theoretical reduction in derivative costs to practical training efficiency.
icml-2026-a-fully-first-order-layer-for-.tldr: FFOLayer trains through optimization problems using first-order gradient estimates, reducing computation while retaining similar reported convergence.

paragraphs: Hypergraph clustering learns groups of nodes using relationships that can connect multiple nodes at once. Many existing methods propagate information through these relationships in a fixed way, implicitly expecting connected nodes to have similar characteristics. That expectation can be misleading in heterophilic data, where connected nodes differ, and can weaken the resulting clusters.

Uni-DHC makes the propagation process learnable. It combines information from multiple orders of relationships and learns how much each should contribute from the data itself. Two additional constraints support unsupervised learning: consistency at the node level stabilizes training, while decorrelation at the hyperedge level addresses redundant structure introduced by higher-order aggregation.

The paper explains the difference through spectral filtering. Conventional propagation acts like a fixed low-pass filter, whereas Uni-DHC learns a polynomial filter with more adaptable behavior. Experiments cover both homophilic and heterophilic datasets and report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with especially strong gains in heterophilic settings. These findings support adapting propagation to the relationship structure rather than fixing it in advance.
icml-2026-a-unified-framework-for-deep-h.tldr: Uni-DHC learns how to combine hypergraph relationships, improving clustering especially when connected nodes have different characteristics.

paragraphs: A training-time backdoor defense can try to recover a clean portion of a poisoned dataset and train on that portion. This paper formulates that strategy as coreset selection: choosing a smaller set of informative examples that supports the intended task while excluding examples associated with the backdoor.

The approach relies on two stated properties of poisonous samples: they are less frequent than benign examples and have lower prediction uncertainty. The authors use cumulative entropy to track uncertainty across learning, helping selection favor informative benign samples. They also unlearn selected examples during each epoch, a step intended to make benign and poisonous examples easier to separate as training proceeds.

Together, these mechanisms construct a benign coreset for training a model without the backdoor. The paper reports consistent mitigation of backdoor attacks with negligible effects on natural task performance. Its contribution is to connect security filtering with informative subset selection: the selected data should both avoid the malicious behavior and retain useful material for learning the legitimate task.
icml-2026-anti-backdoor-coreset-selectio.tldr: Cumulative entropy guides selection of informative benign training examples to mitigate backdoors with little reported loss in normal performance.

paragraphs: Human attention modeling predicts which parts of sensory content attract attention. Existing approaches are often specialized for particular scenes, modalities, or task definitions, making broader application difficult. The Attend to Anything Model, or AAM, brings image, video, and audiovisual attention tasks into a shared multimodal framework.

AAM organizes attention through a hierarchy from general concepts to specific ones. Language prompts express these relationships, and hierarchical embeddings in hyperbolic space represent their structure. To connect still images with changing video, the model also treats attention across frames as a process that evolves over time. This evolution is formulated using the Fokker–Planck equation from a fluid-dynamics perspective.

These choices address both differences between attention tasks and the temporal behavior of attention in video. Across 16 benchmarks, the paper reports an average improvement of 6% over state-of-the-art methods and approximately fourfold faster video inference. The results support a shared modeling approach across the evaluated scenarios, combining a common representation of attention with an explicit account of how it changes over time.
icml-2026-attend-to-anything-foundation-.tldr: AAM unifies image, video, and audiovisual attention modeling through hierarchical language representations and temporal diffusion.

paragraphs: Many backdoors implanted in language models disappear when users subsequently perform supervised fine-tuning. This paper investigates that observation geometrically by measuring how the backdoor objective changes under controlled perturbations to model weights. Conventional poisoning often produces a narrow region in parameter space where the backdoor remains effective.

If that region is sharp and narrow, relatively modest changes during downstream training can move the model outside it, causing the backdoor to be forgotten. The proposed attack, BAD-BOOM, instead encourages a broader, smoother region of low backdoor loss. It extends sharpness-aware minimization with a Fisher-based ellipsoidal constraint that gives backdoor-sensitive parameters larger perturbation budgets.

The evaluation spans two threat settings, three attack scenarios, three open-source language models, and three downstream fine-tuning tasks without triggers. BAD-BOOM consistently retains high attack success rates while maintaining competitive model utility in these experiments. The findings connect backdoor persistence to the geometry surrounding the learned parameters and show why downstream fine-tuning may remove conventional backdoors yet leave deliberately broadened ones effective.
icml-2026-broadening-the-backdoor-basin-.tldr: The paper links backdoor forgetting to narrow loss basins and demonstrates an attack that broadens them to survive downstream fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Combining several language-model judges can seem like a straightforward way to obtain more reliable evaluations. But judges may share preferences for verbosity or style, or inherit similar training artifacts. Their mistakes can therefore be correlated, allowing averaging or majority voting to preserve or amplify the same systematic error.

CARE models each judge's score as a mixture of an underlying quality signal and shared confounding factors. It aims to separate those components without ground-truth labels, rather than simply adjusting how much weight each judge receives. This directly addresses the possibility that agreement among judges reflects a common bias instead of agreement about true quality.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for identifying and recovering the modeled signals under shared confounders, along with an analysis of bias when aggregation omits those factors. Across 12 public benchmarks covering numerical scores, binary decisions, and pairwise preferences, CARE improves aggregation accuracy and reduces error by up to 26.8%. The findings show the value of modeling why judges agree when combining their assessments.
icml-2026-care-confounder-aware-aggregat.tldr: CARE separates shared judge biases from latent quality signals, improving LLM evaluation aggregation without ground-truth labels.

paragraphs: When objects have several views or feature sets, missing views damage both their available features and the relationships used to cluster them. Existing graph approaches may fill in missing data at substantial cost or combine relationships with shallow filters that struggle to separate shared structure from view-specific variation.

CARD instead builds a unified hypergraph from observed relationships between samples and representative anchors. A higher-order resolvent diffusion operator then filters this structure, strengthening the relative contribution of modes dominated by agreement across views while suppressing view-specific variations. The method refines relationships without explicitly reconstructing missing views.

A compact implicit solver connects similarity learning with clustering while avoiding dense matrices. The theoretical refinement analysis is local and conditional on spectral-gap and local-stability assumptions. Experiments on eight benchmarks, including large datasets, report competitive clustering performance. With the anchor budget fixed, the method scales linearly with the number of samples. Together, these results support structural refinement as a scalable way to handle incomplete views without a separate imputation stage.
icml-2026-contractive-anchor-resolvent-d.tldr: CARD refines shared relationships for incomplete multi-view clustering without filling in missing views, scaling linearly with sample count at a fixed anchor budget.

paragraphs: Scientific papers communicate evidence through figures as well as text, creating multiple routes for manipulating automated reviewers. An attack may aim to inflate a paper's score rather than cause a general safety violation. The paper argues that text-only robustness studies leave this domain-specific, multimodal problem insufficiently examined.

PaperGuard combines a peer-review dataset spanning scientific domains with attacks against both textual and visual content. Its attack suite includes black-box prompt injections and white-box perturbations, enabling evaluation across different levels of attacker access. This makes the benchmark address targeted review failures through multiple parts of a paper rather than treating the document as text alone.

The framework also introduces a defense tailored to the long context of academic papers. It searches embeddings of document chunks to locate and mitigate harmful instructions efficiently. Experiments across state-of-the-art models find widespread vulnerability among AI reviewers. The contribution is therefore both an evaluation framework and a practical defense mechanism for studying how manipulated paper content can distort automated scholarly assessment.
icml-2026-does-ai-reviewer-see-the-full-.tldr: PaperGuard benchmarks attacks through paper text and figures and introduces a chunk-search defense for automated peer review.

paragraphs: Selecting a smaller 3D training dataset is complicated by class imbalance in both training and testing. Overall accuracy gives common classes more influence, while mean accuracy emphasizes balanced performance across classes. Consequently, the best subset can depend on which class distribution the evaluation is intended to represent.

The paper views pruning as approximating population risk with a selected set of samples. It separates error into two sources: how well the subset represents the data's underlying geometry and how much its class prior differs from the desired distribution. To address the latter, it separates likelihood from prior and transfers structural information through a calibrated teacher, distillation, and geometry-preserving constraints.

For representation quality, the method selects using geometric embeddings and establishes a safety floor that captures regions useful across priors. A steering wrapper then moves between class-stratified seeding and global selection. The paper explicitly recognizes that no single subset optimally serves divergent evaluation priors. Its experiments report a stronger performance floor while preserving flexibility to accommodate different preferences about class balance.
icml-2026-exploring-3d-dataset-pruning-e.tldr: The framework prunes 3D datasets by separating geometric coverage from class-prior mismatch and allowing selection to follow different evaluation priorities.

paragraphs: Training can favor particular regression solutions even when that preference is not written explicitly into the objective. This paper studies that implicit bias in diagonal linear networks, focusing on gradient flow and initialization values approaching zero. The goal is to characterize both the path followed during learning and the solution selected by that path.

The analysis extends an earlier result to deep diagonal linear networks and a broader specified class of two-layer diagonal networks. For both architectures, the authors show that a proposed algorithm equivalently characterizes the training trajectories. They then prove that this algorithm converges to the solution of a modified l1-norm minimization problem.

That convergence result identifies the networks' implicit preference with a modified l1 norm in the infinitesimal-initialization regime. The paper also identifies the Structural Invariant Manifold as the geometric structure shaping these dynamics. Its contribution is a connection between training trajectories, their underlying geometry, and a precise optimization characterization of the eventual solution for the network classes studied.
icml-2026-gradient-flow-dynamics-and-imp.tldr: For specified diagonal linear networks with infinitesimal initialization, gradient flow selects solutions characterized by modified l1-norm minimization.

paragraphs: Coding agents can implement feature requests with little human supervision, but functional success does not establish that the resulting software is secure. This paper examines that gap using SUSVIBES, a benchmark built from real open-source development tasks where human programmers previously committed vulnerable implementations.

The benchmark contains 186 feature-request tasks, and the evaluation covers 12 coding-agent settings using frontier models. All evaluated agents perform poorly on software security. One reported example makes the gap concrete: SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet produces functionally correct solutions for 57% of tasks, while only 11.8% of its solutions are secure.

The authors also test preliminary security strategies, including adding vulnerability hints to feature requests, and find that these do not mitigate the observed problems. Because the benchmark centers on tasks associated with vulnerable human implementations, its results specifically expose security difficulties in that setting. The findings raise concerns about deploying lightly supervised agent-generated code, especially for security-sensitive applications, and show why functional correctness alone is an insufficient evaluation target.
icml-2026-is-vibe-coding-safe-benchmarki.tldr: SUSVIBES finds a substantial gap between functional correctness and security in coding-agent solutions to real-world feature requests.

paragraphs: Self-evolving agents collect past experience with the aim of improving future behavior. But storing or presenting that experience does not establish that it actually influences decisions. This paper studies experience faithfulness: whether an agent's behavior causally depends on the experience supplied to it.

The authors intervene on both raw experience and condensed versions of it, examining four agent frameworks across 13 language-model backbones and nine environments. They find a consistent asymmetry. Agents depend on raw experience, but often ignore or misinterpret condensed experience, including when the condensed form is the only experience available. The gap appears in both single-agent and multi-agent configurations and across model scales.

The analysis attributes this behavior to limitations in the meaning preserved by condensed content, internal processing biases that suppress experience, and tasks where pretrained knowledge already suffices. These findings question whether accumulated summaries reliably drive improvement. They also distinguish having a memory mechanism from using its contents faithfully, making causal tests of experience use central to assessing self-evolving agents.
icml-2026-large-language-model-agents-ar.tldr: Controlled interventions show that self-evolving agents often use raw experience but disregard or misinterpret condensed experience.

paragraphs: Transformers for partial differential equations often divide space into uniform patches, assigning similar processing effort everywhere. Yet a solution may contain sharp changes, transient features, or structures at several scales. Uniform tokenization can therefore devote detail to relatively uninformative regions while inadequately representing more demanding ones.

MeshTok adapts ideas from adaptive mesh refinement to token construction on a fixed simulation grid. It creates finer tokens in selected regions and coarser tokens elsewhere. All tokens enter one Transformer sequence, allowing global context and local detail to be processed together without specialized architectural components.

Adaptive refinement moderately increases the token count, so the method's rationale is a more targeted allocation of computation rather than an automatic reduction in tokens. The authors explicitly frame this as a practical inductive bias, without a formal optimality guarantee. Across multiple PDE families and benchmark datasets, MeshTok consistently improves the reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off over uniform-grid baselines. These results suggest that choosing spatial representation scales adaptively can improve neural PDE modeling.
icml-2026-meshtok-efficient-multi-scale-.tldr: MeshTok allocates finer spatial tokens to informative PDE regions, improving the reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning can improve visual reasoning scores while leaving models susceptible to misleading text. This paper tests controlled perturbations such as incorrect captions and erroneous reasoning traces. These cause substantial robustness drops, with weaknesses becoming more pronounced when evaluation also considers consistency of the model's chain of thought.

Open-source multimodal reasoning models show particularly strong vulnerabilities. Closed models exhibit similar failures but retain greater robustness and reasoning consistency, suggesting that current fine-tuning methods contribute to the gap. Analysis of training dynamics reveals an accuracy–faithfulness trade-off: higher benchmark accuracy can coincide with less reliable explanations and weaker robustness to contextual changes.

The paper also examines proposed remedies. Adversarial augmentation improves robustness but does not alone prevent reasoning from drifting away from faithful explanations. A faithfulness-aware reward can realign answers and reasoning, yet combining it with augmentation risks training collapse toward shortcut strategies. These results motivate evaluating and training for correctness, robustness, and reasoning consistency together, because improvement on one dimension can conceal deterioration on another.
icml-2026-on-robustness-and-chain-of-tho.tldr: RL fine-tuning can improve visual reasoning accuracy while weakening reasoning faithfulness and robustness to misleading textual context.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models save computation by activating only a few experts for each token. Training the selection mechanism is difficult because choosing a discrete subset does not directly support ordinary differentiation. ProbMoE addresses this by representing routing as a probability distribution over expert subsets with constraints on their size.

In Exact-k routing, the forward computation samples a subset containing exactly k experts. During the backward computation, the method differentiates through each expert's exact marginal probability of selection. Those derivatives provide a tractable surrogate for the true routing gradient; the exactness applies to the marginal probabilities, not to the surrogate being the true gradient.

The framework also supports Dynamic-k routing, allowing the number of selected experts to vary within the same predefined range during training and inference. Across evaluated benchmarks and model backbones, Exact-k delivers strong performance alongside better expert utilization and more diverse routing. Dynamic-k achieves comparable performance while activating fewer experts. Together, the results support probabilistic subset modeling as a way to train both fixed and adaptive expert allocation.
icml-2026-probmoe-differentiable-probabi.tldr: ProbMoE uses distributions over expert subsets to train fixed or adaptive routing with tractable gradient surrogates.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models activate only a small fraction of their experts for an input, but deployment still requires storing all expert parameters. Removing or merging whole experts can reduce memory needs while damaging performance, particularly under heavy compression. PuzzleMoE targets redundancy at the finer level of individual weight elements.

Its sparse merging procedure uses two masks to capture both parameters that can be shared and salient parameters specific to individual experts. This allows compression to reflect differences within experts instead of treating each expert or tensor as one indivisible unit. Preserving expert-specific elements is part of the method's approach to maintaining accuracy.

Fine-grained merging also creates storage and execution overhead from masks and signs. PuzzleMoE addresses this with a bit-packed encoding that reuses underutilized exponent bits for efficient GPU inference. Experiments report improvements over prior compression methods of up to 16.7% on MMLU at a 50% compression ratio, along with up to 1.80-fold end-to-end throughput gains. The contribution combines a finer compression decision with an encoding designed to make that decision computationally useful.
icml-2026-puzzlemoe-efficient-compressio.tldr: PuzzleMoE combines element-wise expert merging with bit-packed storage to improve compressed MoE accuracy and inference throughput.

paragraphs: Some language-model abilities appear to improve abruptly as model scale increases, despite smoother overall scaling trends. Explanations have included capabilities becoming available at a particular scale and evaluation metrics creating artificial thresholds. This paper investigates a different source of apparent breakthroughs: variation in training outcomes across random seeds.

The authors examine synthetic length generalization, multiple-choice question answering, and grammatical generalization. Different seeds can yield either smooth improvement or apparently emergent behavior. The paper connects sharp metric changes to continuous shifts in the distribution of outcomes across seeds, especially when that distribution has two distinct modes.

The distribution itself may become abruptly bimodal at a capacity threshold, but that threshold appears well before most seeds achieve a breakthrough. The observed effects also persist with continuous loss metrics, so they cannot be explained solely by thresholded evaluation scores. These findings make random training variation relevant to scaling predictions: a model's size can affect the likelihood of reaching a capability, while individual runs need not display the same progression.
icml-2026-random-scaling-of-emergent-cap.tldr: Apparent capability breakthroughs can arise from changing probabilities of training outcomes across random seeds as models scale.

paragraphs: Causal language modeling predicts using preceding context, even though later text is available in the training data. Regret Pre-training uses that future information as a teaching signal. A single model produces a causal student distribution and a teacher distribution that has access to additional context.

Training combines ordinary language modeling with a regret loss that reduces the divergence from the teacher distribution to the student distribution. LocalRegret gives the teacher attention to one future token. GlobalRegret provides bidirectional context while masking the target position. Both configurations transfer future-aware information into representations used by the causal student.

On OLMoE-1B-7B after four billion training tokens, both configurations outperform the baseline across nine downstream tasks. Average accuracy reaches 33.9% for GlobalRegret and 32.2% for LocalRegret, compared with 30.2% for the baseline. GlobalRegret's BoolQ improvement is 18.1 percentage points. The framework adds no parameters and requires one additional inference-mode forward pass per training step, making richer training context available through extra computation rather than a separate teacher model.
icml-2026-regret-pre-training-bridging-p.tldr: Regret Pre-training lets one model teach its causal predictions using future-aware training context, improving reported downstream accuracy without adding parameters.

paragraphs: Reasoning training depends on having sufficiently challenging and varied problems. Human-written collections are expensive and limited, while synthetic collections can be too easy or narrow. PromptScale builds on rationale-guided problem synthesis, replacing handcrafted heuristics with an expectation-maximization loop that repeatedly refines the rationales used to construct prompts.

The generated prompts support two training settings. Strong models use self-play with verifiable feedback and no stronger teacher. Weaker models use supervised fine-tuning with reasoning traces distilled from a teacher. This separates the production of challenging problems from the choice of how a model learns to solve them.

In self-play, the evaluated Qwen3 model achieves new state-of-the-art results at the 30B scale across the reported mathematics and programming evaluations. In supervised training, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct trained solely on synthetic prompts surpasses compared models trained on human or hybrid data. Further analysis finds that PromptScale's problems are harder and distributionally distinct. The findings support improving the training-problem supply as an additional route to scaling reasoning alongside model size and test-time computation.
icml-2026-scaling-prompt-synthesis-for-l.tldr: PromptScale iteratively refines rationale-guided problem synthesis to produce harder, more diverse training prompts for self-play and supervised reasoning.

paragraphs: On-policy distillation trains a student on reasoning trajectories it generates itself, with a teacher supplying guidance at each token. This helps align training with the situations the student encounters during generation. However, conventional versions typically require a separate teacher and do not explicitly exploit ground-truth solutions already available in reasoning datasets.

On-Policy Self-Distillation uses one language model in two contexts. As the teacher, it sees privileged information; as the student, it receives only the question. Training reduces the per-token divergence between their distributions along the student's own rollouts. The teaching advantage therefore comes from additional context rather than a separate, larger model.

The approach is motivated by the idea that a sufficiently capable model can interpret external reasoning traces and use them to guide its less-informed self. Across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the paper reports better token efficiency than reinforcement-learning methods and better performance than off-policy distillation methods. These findings support combining privileged solution information with feedback on the model's own generated trajectories.
icml-2026-self-distilled-reasoner-on-pol.tldr: OPSD lets a model teach itself on its own reasoning rollouts by giving its teacher context privileged solution information.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer a Bayesian approach to prediction and uncertainty estimation, but their computational demands make large-scale use difficult. SIKA-GP addresses this bottleneck by approximating kernels with sparse inducing representations. The goal is to retain expressive kernel models while reducing the computation needed to use them.

The method builds on a dyadic ordered template basis, activating only a sparse set of basis elements. Its complexity dependence on the number of inducing points is logarithmic. Compact representations also support tensorized GPU computation and integration with large models, connecting the mathematical approximation to an implementation suited to modern hardware.

SIKA-GP can be embedded in Bayesian neural networks with sparse activations and extends to deep feature learning with high-dimensional representations. The paper reports substantial training and inference speedups without sacrificing predictive performance. Evaluations on vision and Transformer-based language benchmarks consistently produce fast, accurate Gaussian-process models. These findings support sparse kernel representations as a practical route for carrying Bayesian kernel methods into larger learned-feature systems.
icml-2026-sika-gp-accelerating-gaussian-.tldr: SIKA-GP uses sparse kernel bases with logarithmic dependence on inducing-point count to accelerate Gaussian-process models and Bayesian deep learning.

paragraphs: Improving a policy from a fixed dataset requires balancing better actions against staying close to behavior supported by the data. Weighted regression can be overly cautious about valuable but uncommon actions. Direct value-gradient updates can instead conflict with data fitting and push a policy away from the data manifold.

SPAR anchors learning to a frozen policy trained by pure behavior cloning. It learns local residual corrections around that reference, narrowing the space in which fitting and improvement take place. This turns policy improvement into adjusting an existing behavior locally rather than searching globally for an entirely new policy.

Within the residual space, Latent Self-Imitation uses latent sampling and weighted regression to address conflicting fitting and improvement gradients. The paper proves that this mechanism eliminates the component of standard value-gradient drift normal to the data manifold. Experiments on D4RL report substantial improvements from suboptimal baselines and state-of-the-art performance. The combined contribution is a constrained local improvement framework and a learning mechanism designed to keep improvement aligned with data-supported behavior.
icml-2026-spar-support-preserving-action.tldr: SPAR improves offline policies through local corrections to frozen behavior cloning, using latent self-imitation to avoid drift away from data-supported actions.

paragraphs: Offline meta-reinforcement learning seeks to transfer learning from fixed datasets to previously unseen tasks. Expert-based methods must decide which specialists should handle a new task, but routing based on individual tokens or short trajectory fragments can miss broader relationships between tasks. The Task-Guided Router makes those relationships explicit.

TGR represents tasks using several complementary views: semantic descriptions, summaries of behavior, and latent features describing dynamics. Its routing mechanism uses these representations to assess global task compatibility and assign experts accordingly. This structure is intended to support stable specialization while allowing useful knowledge to transfer between related tasks.

Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art offline meta-reinforcement-learning methods in few-shot generalization. The gains are especially evident when data are sparse and dynamics differ across tasks. These findings support task-level information as a useful routing prior: deciding which experts fit the overall task can improve transfer when local observations provide an incomplete or fragmented picture of what the agent needs to do.
icml-2026-structured-expert-routing-with.tldr: TGR routes experts using semantic, behavioral, and dynamics-based task representations to improve few-shot offline reinforcement-learning generalization.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can collaborate as specialists across stages of a workflow, but the training data for those roles may belong to different organizations. Privacy, intellectual-property, and compliance constraints can prevent pooling that data. Federated learning keeps data local, yet conventional approaches often treat participating clients independently and overlook dependencies between workflow stages.

FedWave incorporates those dependencies into federated collaboration. A Value Chain Layer models relationships between stages, while federated LoRA adaptation maintains role-specific expertise. A shared mixture-of-experts router combines experts according to the input. A subsequent Direct Preference Optimization stage uses preferences induced by that router.

The framework therefore connects local specialist adaptation with coordination across the sequence of tasks. Experiments across workflow datasets and language-model backbones show improvements over federated baselines while remaining competitive with centralized multi-agent systems. These results support workflow-aware learning when data must stay distributed: preserving local data access can coexist with useful coordination between experts whose contributions depend on earlier and later stages.
icml-2026-weaving-in-the-clouds-achievin.tldr: FedWave combines federated specialist adaptation with workflow-aware routing to coordinate LLM agents while keeping training data local.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce training images exactly or nearly exactly, raising privacy and copyright concerns. GUARD addresses this during image generation by modifying denoising guidance. Its attractive–repulsive formulation steers generation away from an original training image and toward a distinct image that remains consistent with the text prompt.

The paper instantiates that framework with targeted cross-attention attenuation. A statistical mechanism identifies which positions in each prompt need reduced cross-attention, and attenuation is applied at those locations. The resulting positive target gives the generation process a prompt-specific direction to move toward while avoiding reproduction of the training image.

Because the intervention is dynamic and applied at inference time, its attention adjustments depend on the individual prompt. Across two architectures, the authors report consistently state-of-the-art memorization mitigation for both verbatim and template memorization. Image quality is improved or comparable in the reported evaluations. The findings support selectively adjusting the prompt's influence during denoising as a way to reduce memorization while preserving useful alignment and visual quality.
icml-2026-you-dont-need-all-that-attenti.tldr: GUARD selectively attenuates prompt cross-attention during generation to reduce image memorization while maintaining or improving reported image quality.
